title: Treat non-String messages as invalid in MessageVerifier and MessageEncryptor
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because `ActiveSupport::MessageVerifier` raises `NoMethodError` when the message is not a String. `extract_encoded` guards only against `nil` before calling `valid_encoding?`, so an `Array`, a `Hash` or `ActionController::Parameters` blows up in `verified`, `verify` and `valid_message?` instead of being rejected as invalid.

These values come straight from untrusted request parameters. `ActiveStorage::SetBlob` passes `params[:signed_blob_id] || params[:signed_id]` to `find_signed!` and rescues only `InvalidSignature`, so this request answers 500 instead of 404:

```text
GET /rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/x/y.png?signed_blob_id[]=a
NoMethodError: undefined method 'valid_encoding?' for an instance of Array
```

The same applies to any `find_signed`, `verified` or `verify` call fed a parameter that a client can turn into an array or a hash.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `MessageVerifier#extract_encoded` to treat any non-String message as an invalid message format, exactly like a malformed string: `verified` returns `nil`, `valid_message?` returns `false` and `verify` raises `InvalidSignature`.

`MessageEncryptor` in AEAD mode never reaches the verifier and had the same gap in `extract_parts` (`NoMethodError` or `ArgumentError`, also for `nil`). It now throws `:invalid_message_format` there, so `decrypt_and_verify` raises `InvalidMessage`. In non-AEAD mode the message goes through the verifier first and is covered by the change above.

### Additional information

The check lives in the verifier and encryptor rather than in each caller (Active Storage, Active Record signed IDs, cookies), so every caller gets the same behaviour.

title: Fix Active Job errors not being logged at :warn and :error
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because a failing job logs nothing when the log level is `:warn` or `:error`. "Error performing" is written at `:error`, but since #45796 (Rails 7.1) its handler is only run when the logger is at `:info` or below, and `event_log_level :completed, :info` kept that on main. The same goes for the "Failed enqueuing" logged when the adapter raises. Apps logging at `:warn` in production lose exactly the lines they kept that level for. It's the same kind of bug as #58959 for CSRF warnings.

### Detail

This Pull Request declares `completed`, `enqueued` and `enqueued_at` at `:error`, as `step` already is. Their success lines still go through `info`, so they are only written at `:info` and below. With `verbose_enqueue_logs`, the enqueue source is now only looked up when its line would be written, so the handlers running at `:warn` don't walk the stack for nothing.

The trade-off: at `:warn` and `:error`, these events are now built for every job, not only failing ones, since `consumes?` only knows the event name. That's 7 more objects and about 2 µs per job. `step` already pays it, and avoiding it would take a separate failure event or a payload-aware `consumes?`. It also takes back the Active Job part of what #58957 gains at `:warn`, since that part came from skipping these same handlers.

### Additional information

<details>
<summary>Per-job cost, main (a7776a6) → this PR, Ruby 4.0.9, median of 7</summary>

| | interpreter | YJIT | objects |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| enqueue, `:info` | within noise | within noise | 112 → 112 |
| execute, `:info` | within noise | within noise | 206 → 206 |
| enqueue, `:warn` | 16.1 → 18.0 µs | 16.8 → 18.8 µs | 105 → 112 |
| execute, `:warn` | 23.2 → 24.6 µs | 23.2 → 24.9 µs | 192 → 199 |
| enqueue, `:error` | 16.6 → 18.2 µs | 17.9 → 19.6 µs | 105 → 112 |
| execute, `:error` | 23.5 → 24.5 µs | 24.2 → 26.8 µs | 192 → 199 |

Enqueue is `perform_later` with a JSON adapter, execute is `ActiveJob::Base.execute` on the parsed payload, in a production app.

</details>

Failures of `perform_all_later` are still logged at `:info` whatever the level, I left that for a separate PR.

title: Run Action Cable async subscriber map changes in order
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because, on the async adapter, subscribing and unsubscribing a stream can run out of order. A stream started during a subscribe that is then rejected can stay registered, and the rejected client keeps receiving that stream's broadcasts.

```ruby
class RoomChannel < ApplicationCable::Channel
  def subscribed
    reject unless current_user.can_access?(params[:room])
    stream_from "room_#{params[:room]}"
  end
end
```

The client is sent `reject_subscription` and the subscription is removed, but the handler registered by `stream_from` can survive. A later `ActionCable.server.broadcast("room_...", ...)` is still transmitted to that client, an `unsubscribe` from the client does not remove the handler, and it stays after the socket closes. `stream_from` followed by `reject` behaves the same way, and so does any subscribe that is undone straight away.

The cause is in `SubscriberMap::Async`, which posts every `add_subscriber` and `remove_subscriber` to the server's executor as a separate task. The executor is a pool of up to ten threads, so a removal can run before the addition it follows. It then finds nothing to remove, and the addition registers the subscriber afterwards.

Related:
- #50979 made unsubscribing asynchronous for the async adapter, which is when removals became tasks of their own.
- #57697 describes this reordering and makes the removal tolerate an unknown channel, but the subscriber added afterwards still stays.
- #59371 orders one connection's commands, which does not order the tasks the adapter posts afterwards.
- #53101 skips `subscribed` after a rejection in `before_subscribe`; it is not part of this problem.

### Detail

This Pull Request posts `SubscriberMap::Async`'s `add_subscriber` and `remove_subscriber` through a `Concurrent::SerializedExecution`, so a map runs them one at a time in the order they were requested. They still run on the executor's threads, and `invoke_callback` is unchanged.

Tests, each of which fails without the change:

- `SubscriberMapTest`: with an executor that runs the tasks it is given newest first (`OutOfOrderExecutor`, a new stub), a subscriber that is added and then removed is still registered and receives a broadcast.
- `ActionCable::Channel::RejectionTest`: the same executor behind the async adapter, with a channel that calls `reject` before `stream_from` and one that calls it after. Without the change the rejected connection is sent the broadcast.

### Additional information

Real Puma and raw WebSocket clients on 127.0.0.1, async adapter, 150 connections per case, on `main` without and with this change. "Later broadcast" is the number of rejected clients that received a broadcast sent after their rejection; handlers are counted in the adapter's subscriber map after all sockets were closed.

| channel | later broadcast, before | after | handlers left, before | after |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| `reject unless ...` then `stream_from` | 10 | 0 | 10 | 0 |
| `stream_from` then `reject` | 12 | 0 | 12 | 0 |
| `return reject unless ...` then `stream_from` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

An allowed subscriber was confirmed, received the broadcast, and left no handler after closing, with and without the change. Some clients did not get a reject or confirm frame within the driver's 3 second wait; the counts above are of the clients that did receive the broadcast or left a handler. The numbers vary from run to run because they depend on thread scheduling.

Not covered:
- The Redis and PostgreSQL adapters add subscribers in the calling thread; I did not run them.
- `stream_from` followed by `reject` still has a short window in which the handler is live before `reject_subscription` stops the streams.
- 8-1-stable is not affected by this change; see the comment below about whether a separate fix is wanted there.

title: Inspect the invalid value in the enum `ArgumentError` message
body:
### Motivation / Background

Assigning a value that is not a member of an enum raises an `ArgumentError` whose message interpolates the value directly:

    raise ArgumentError, "'#{value}' is not a valid #{name}. Valid values are: ..."

The value commonly comes from request parameters, for example `Post.new(params.expect(post: [:status]))`. `ArgumentError` is not a rescued response, so the request fails with a 500 and `ActionDispatch::DebugExceptions` writes the exception message to the log. A value carrying ANSI escape sequences or newlines is written verbatim.

This is a hardening change in the same class as [CVE-2025-55193](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-76r7-hhxj-r776), which added `.inspect` to the ids in `RecordNotFound` messages, and its follow-up in #58187 for nested attributes.

### Detail

This change calls `.inspect` on the value before interpolating it. Strings are now double quoted with their control bytes escaped to inert text, and symbols are shown as symbols:

```ruby
Book.new(status: "bogus")
# before: ArgumentError: 'bogus' is not a valid status. Valid values are: "proposed", "written", "published"
# after:  ArgumentError: "bogus" is not a valid status. Valid values are: "proposed", "written", "published"

Book.new(status: :bogus)
# before: ArgumentError: 'bogus' is not a valid status. ...
# after:  ArgumentError: :bogus is not a valid status. ...
```

A value of `"\e[31mHello\e[0m"` (containing raw ANSI escape bytes) previously passed through to the message verbatim. It now renders as the quoted, inert literal `"\e[31mHello\e[0m"`.

Only enums that raise on invalid values are affected, which is the default. Enums declared with `validate: true` do not raise.

### Additional information

The message format changes for every caller, so code matching on the old single-quoted form would need updating. The valid values in the same message are already rendered with `inspect`, so the invalid value now matches them.

The list of valid values was added to this message in #57446, which has not been released yet. Rather than add a second CHANGELOG entry, I updated the example in that entry and in the PostgreSQL guide to show the new format. I'm happy to add a separate entry if you'd prefer one.

I reported this privately first (GHSA-f2mv-fv8j-x38m). It was closed as informative, as log injection is treated as hardening, with an invitation to open the patch here.

title: Keep the password reset token out of the path
body:
### Motivation / Background

`bin/rails generate authentication` adds `resources :passwords, param: :token`, so the reset link is `/passwords/<token>/edit` and the form submits to `PUT /passwords/<token>`.

Rails filters sensitive values in the `Parameters:` log line, and it filters query string values (`config.filter_parameters`) in `request.filtered_path` and in the `Redirected to` line. It does not filter path segments. Because the token is a path segment, it appears in clear text in the request and redirect log lines of a newly generated app (production logs at `info`):

    Started GET "/passwords/<token>/edit" for ...
    Started PUT "/passwords/<token>" for ...
    Redirected to http://.../passwords/<token>/edit      (when the passwords do not match)

The `Parameters:` line of the same requests shows `"token" => "[FILTERED]"`, so the generated app already treats `token` as sensitive; the path is the one place it is not covered. The token is valid for 15 minutes and is not invalidated by being used.

Related public work on log filtering: #59314 (merged) matches decoded query parameter names, #59216 and #59395 (open) extend query string filtering, #59592 (open) filters redirects declared in `routes.rb`. These concern query strings and redirect routes; none changes how path segments are handled. #53060 / #53087 (closed) discussed the token in the URL because of the `Referer` header; this PR is about the log lines, not `Referer`, and does not store the token in the session.

### Detail

The generator now defines `resource :password, only: [ :new, :create, :edit, :update ]` and passes the token as a query parameter: `/password/edit?token=...` and `PUT /password?token=...`. The existing query string filtering then covers the `Started` and `Redirected to` lines. The controller, views, mailer templates and generated tests are updated to match, and so is the route shown in `guides/source/sign_up_and_settings.md`. In newly generated apps the `passwords_path` helper becomes `password_path`, and the token helpers take `token:`.

Filtering path parameters in the framework would be the more general fix, but the `Started` line is written by `Rails::Rack::Logger` before routing, so the path parameters are not known yet, and `filtered_path` is memoized and reused in later payloads. Changing that means moving the line after routing, which is a larger change (see #58889 and the discussion in #49245). This PR only changes the code Rails generates.

Tests: `railties/test/generators/authentication_generator_test.rb` passes (10 runs). The new test, and the updated routes assertion, fail without the change. I also ran a generated app (8.1.4.1, production environment) with the same edits applied: the reset flow works, the generated controller tests pass, and the server log shows `/password/edit?token=[FILTERED]`, `/password?token=[FILTERED]` and `Redirected to .../password/edit?token=[FILTERED]` with no occurrence of the token.

### Additional information

Only newly generated applications are affected; existing applications keep their current routes. An existing app that copies this change would invalidate reset links already emailed to users (they expire after 15 minutes anyway).

Not addressed here: other path segments that carry secrets are still logged unfiltered, and the token is still part of the URL (now as a query parameter).

title: Detect N+1 queries in collections with `:n_plus_one_only` mode
body:
Closes [#56094][]


### Motivation / Background

Prior to this commit, configuring Active Record to strict load by default in `:n_plus_one_only` mode did not raise when lazily loading an association for each record in a collection:

```ruby
Post.strict_loading_by_default = true
Post.strict_loading_mode = :n_plus_one_only

Post.all.each { |post| post.comments.map(&:body) }
```

Despite the absence of a `StrictLoadingViolationError`, the log includes an N+1 query:

```
Post Load (0.0ms)  SELECT "posts".* FROM "posts"
Comment Load (0.0ms)  SELECT "comments".* FROM "comments" WHERE "comments"."post_id" = ?  [["post_id", 1]]
Comment Load (0.0ms)  SELECT "comments".* FROM "comments" WHERE "comments"."post_id" = ?  [["post_id", 2]]
```

### Detail

When in `:n_plus_one_only`, a record raises a
`StrictLoadingViolationError` When lazily loading a `has_many` association. The records'

Records loaded through a `has_many` association are switched to `:all` mode by `ActiveRecord::Associations::Association#set_strict_loading`.

Records loaded directly from an `ActiveRecord::Relation` are not, and remain in `:n_plus_one_only` mode. As a result, they never raise when lazily loading their own associations.

This commit sets records to `:n_plus_one_only` mode when a query loads them from a collection with more than one record. The `strict_loading_mode` does not change, so lazily loading a record's `belongs_to` and `has_one` associations continue to behave as they did before.

Queries that load a single record (like `first`, `find`, `find_by`, and `sole`) do not change the record's mode. Relations that declare a `strict_loading` value skip the check.

[#56094]: https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/56094

### Additional information

The reproduction script from the original issue:

```ruby

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", "~> 8.1.1"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"

  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  config.active_record.encryption.primary_key = "primary_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.deterministic_key = "deterministic_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.key_derivation_salt = "key_derivation_salt"

  config.active_record.strict_loading_by_default = true
  config.active_record.strict_loading_mode = :n_plus_one_only
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
    t.text :name
  end

  create_table :comments, force: true do |t|
    t.text :body
    t.integer :post_id
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :comments
end

class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def test_strict_loading_errors_raised
    one, two = Post.create!([ { name: "one" }, { name: "two" } ])
    Comment.create!([
      { body: "one comment", post: one },
      { body: "two comment", post: two }
    ])

    assert_raises match: /`Post` is marked for strict_loading/ do
      Post.all.flat_map { |post| post.comments.map(&:body) }
    end
  end
end
```

title: Keep encrypts in a subclass from adding the attribute to its parent
body:
### Motivation / Background

`encrypts` sets up the list with `self.encrypted_attributes ||= Set.new`. In a subclass the parent's set is already there, so the subclass adds its attributes to the parent's set:

```ruby
class User < ActiveRecord::Base
  encrypts :email
end

class Admin < User
  encrypts :ssn
end

User.encrypted_attributes # => #<Set: {:email, :ssn}>
User.create!(email: "a@b.c", ssn: "1").decrypt
# NoMethodError: undefined method 'encrypted?' for an instance of ActiveModel::Type::String
User.deterministic_encrypted_attributes
# NoMethodError: undefined method 'deterministic?'
```

With `extend_queries` on, the uniqueness validation calls `deterministic_encrypted_attributes`, so `valid?` raises on the parent too.

### Detail

`encrypts` now gives the class its own copy of the set. Attributes the parent encrypts later are passed down to subclasses that already have their own copy, the same way #59492 does for `attr_readonly`, so a subclass still sees everything its parent encrypts.

### Motivation / Background

<!--

If you are fixing a specific issue, include "Fixes #ISSUE" (replace with the issue number, remove the quotes) and the issue will be linked to this PR.

This Pull Request has been created because the current documentation for https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionController/MimeResponds.html#method-i-respond_to suggests that using `format.any` within a `respond_to` block will apply to _any_ other requests that do not match other definitions. This is reinforced by the ordering of the `format.html` and `format.any` lines in the example; a non-matching request would be fairly assumed to have been checked against each block in order, eventually using the `format.any` block (which also happens to be the last block).

However, it's actually the case that requests with a MIME type of `*/*` or lacking an `Accept` header will use the _first-defined_ format, rather than the later `format.any`, based off the implementation of: https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/b90ec616a0c82652a1f74331e094c0c96c5fe130/actionpack/lib/action_dispatch/http/mime_negotiation.rb#L200-L208

Likewise, requests with an empty `Accept` header use the route's configuration to determine the default format, which may also be unexpected, given the notable difference between `Accept: ` and having no header at all. This handling could be considered a bug, depending on one's reading of https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.accept, a route's configuration and implementation, and expected behaviour (perhaps better summarised by https://stackoverflow.com/a/12131993/1048705).

### Detail

This Pull Request changes documentation for `respond_to` in order to explain these situations as the current Rails implementation exists.

title: Fix `has_one :through` configuration errors referring to `has_many`
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because a misconfigured `has_one :through` association is reported as a `has_many :through` one, and following the suggested fix would turn it into a collection.

```ruby
class Owner < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one :pet
  has_one :toy, through: :pet, source: :favorite_toy
end

Owner.new.toy
# => ActiveRecord::HasManyThroughSourceAssociationNotFoundError:
#    Could not find the source association(s) :favorite_toy in model Pet.
#    Try 'has_many :toy, :through => :pet, :source => <name>'. Is it one of owner or toy?
```

Four messages are affected, each raised for `has_one :through` as well as `has_many :through`:

- the source association can't be found (above)
- a `:source_type` is given for a source that is not polymorphic
- the source is polymorphic and there is no `:source_type`
- the association is defined before its `:through` association

### Detail

This Pull Request changes these messages to name the macro the association was defined with. The messages for `has_many :through` associations are unchanged, and so are the error classes.

### Additional information

Where the checks differ, `has_one :through` already has its own wording (`HasOneAssociationPolymorphicThroughError`, `HasOneThroughCantAssociateThroughCollection`).

title: Deprecate a blank `password:` in `http_basic_authenticate_with`
body:
### Motivation / Background

`http_basic_authenticate_with` raises an `ArgumentError` when `password:` is not a String, so a missing credential is caught when the controller loads. An empty String passes that check, and then authenticates any request that sends the configured name with an empty password:

```ruby
http_basic_authenticate_with name: "admin", password: ENV["PASSWORD"].to_s

# With PASSWORD unset:
#   Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46   ("admin:")   => 200
```

`ENV[...].to_s` is a natural way to satisfy the String check, and was the workaround suggested in #45360. A variable that is missing in one environment then silently leaves the action open there.

### Detail

This Pull Request deprecates passing a blank `password:` to `http_basic_authenticate_with`, to be turned into an `ArgumentError` in Rails 8.3, in line with how `nil` is already handled.

A blank `name:` is left alone, since authenticating on the password alone is a legitimate setup. `authenticate_with_http_basic` and `authenticate_or_request_with_http_basic` are unchanged, so the password-less use restored in 9ebfb149ed still works.

### Additional information

I went with a deprecation rather than raising straight away because applications using the `.to_s` workaround would otherwise fail to load in any environment where the variable is unset. Happy to switch to raising immediately if that is preferred.

The first new test covers the existing `nil` check, which had no test.

title: Filter hash job arguments in Active Job events and logs
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because job arguments stopped being filtered in Active Job events between 8.1 and main. I found it while keeping personal data out of an application's job logs.

```ruby
config.filter_parameters += [:token]
InviteJob.perform_later(user, token: "abc123")
# 8.1:  arguments: [#<User>, {token: "[FILTERED]"}]
# main: arguments: [#<User>, {token: "abc123"}]
```

In 8.1 the event reporter filtered every hash payload. #56837 rightly stopped that for framework events, since it also masked internal metadata like SQL query names, but it left job arguments, which are user data, unfiltered.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `ActiveJob::StructuredEventSubscriber` to run job arguments through the event reporter's parameter filter, as 8.1 did. `EventReporter#payload_filter` becomes public (`:nodoc:`) so the subscriber shares the reporter's filter list and reload.

Because the log subscriber builds its lines from these events, the text log is now filtered too, which it never was before. Substring matches apply there as well (`cache_key` with the default `:_key`).

### Additional information

#34438 and #38963 were declined because only hash arguments can be filtered by key. That still holds: positional arguments are logged as given, a test pins it, and the `log_arguments` docs now point such jobs to `log_arguments = false`. The difference now is that 8.1 already filters these events, so apps upgrading would see filtered values reappear. Happy to limit this to the event payload if filtering the text log is unwanted.

title: Return a UTC time from `Time.rfc3339` for the "-00:00" offset
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because Active Support's `Time.rfc3339` returns a time with a fixed "+00:00" offset for the "-00:00" offset, where Ruby's `Time.rfc3339` returns a UTC time.

#58402 made the Active Support definition return a UTC time for the "Z" designator, to converge on Ruby's implementation, which is used instead whenever the `time` gem provides it. That implementation is in `time` 0.5.0, and it returns a UTC time for "-00:00" as well, like `Time.iso8601` and `Time.new` do. So on main the result depends on the version of the `time` gem:

```ruby
Time.rfc3339("2026-08-07T10:00:00-00:00")
# time 0.4.2 (Active Support's definition): 2026-08-07 10:00:00 +0000 (utc? => false)
# time 0.5.0 (Ruby's definition):           2026-08-07 10:00:00 UTC   (utc? => true)

Time.iso8601("2026-08-07T10:00:00-00:00") # => 2026-08-07 10:00:00 UTC
Time.new("2026-08-07T10:00:00-00:00")     # => 2026-08-07 10:00:00 UTC
```

### Detail

This Pull Request makes the Active Support definition return a UTC time for "-00:00" too:

```ruby
Time.rfc3339("2026-08-07T10:00:00-00:00")
# Before: 2026-08-07 10:00:00 +0000 (utc? => false)
# After:  2026-08-07 10:00:00 UTC   (utc? => true)
```

As with "Z", the time value is the same and only its representation changes. "+00:00" still returns a time with a fixed offset, as it does in Ruby (`test_rfc3339_parse_with_numeric_zero_offset`).

The added test passes with either definition. Without the change it fails where Active Support defines the method.

### Additional information

Both results above are from Ruby 4.0.2, with `time` 0.4.2 (its default gem) and with `time` 0.5.0 installed.

The CHANGELOG entry added in #58402 mentions the "Z" designator only. I left it as it is, and I'm happy to extend it if that is preferred.

Tests run in `activesupport`: `bin/test test/core_ext/time_ext_test.rb` (177 runs, 0 failures), `bin/test test/time_zone_test.rb test/core_ext/time_with_zone_test.rb test/core_ext/date_time_ext_test.rb test/json/encoding_test.rb` (1069 runs, 0 failures), and the whole suite (6917 runs, 0 failures).

title: Allow `:dependent` association option to be a Proc
body:
The callable is evaluated against the owner whenever the option is used (destroy, `collection.delete`, has_one replacement) and may return any valid `:dependent` value, or `nil` to leave associated records untouched.

```ruby
has_many :projects, dependent: -> { admin? ? nil : :destroy }
```

### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because `:dependent` can only be a static value today, while what should happen to associated records often depends on the owner's state: keep an admin's projects but destroy everyone else's, archive instead of delete for some tenants, and so on.

The current workaround is to drop `:dependent` and write a custom `before_destroy` callback. That gives up the built-in strategies (`:restrict_with_error`, `:destroy_async` with batching, `:nullify` on polymorphic associations), and `collection.delete` and `has_one` replacement no longer follow the same rule.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `has_many`, `has_one` and `belongs_to` to accept a callable for `:dependent`:

- A zero-arity callable is `instance_exec`'d on the owner. A callable with one argument receives the owner. This matches how association scopes work.
- The callable may return any value valid for that association, or `nil` to do nothing.
- The returned value is validated when it is used. An invalid value raises `ArgumentError` with a hint to return `nil`. A common mistake is returning `:none`, which is not a valid value.
- Because the value is only known at runtime, the destroy and `destroy_async` after-commit callbacks are always installed for a callable, and `:ensuring_owner_was` is accepted alongside it.
- Every place that read `options[:dependent]` now goes through a single `Association#dependent_option`: `handle_dependency` for all three macros, `CollectionAssociation#delete` and `#delete_all`, and `HasOneAssociation#delete` and `#replace`.

### Additional information

- The callable runs every time the option is used, not only on destroy. This includes `collection.delete(record)`, `collection.delete_all` without an argument, and assigning a new record to a `has_one`. This keeps those paths consistent with the static option.
- For `belongs_to`, the callable is evaluated before the target is loaded, so returning `nil` costs no query.
- Static `:dependent` values behave exactly as before, including their error messages.
- Considered and rejected: adding a `:none` value. `nil` already means "do nothing" for the static option, and `-> { :destroy unless admin? }` reads naturally.

title: Fix `edit_polymorphic_path` skipping an overridden `polymorphic_path`
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because, on main, `edit_polymorphic_path`, `new_polymorphic_path` and their `_url` counterparts no longer go through `polymorphic_path` / `polymorphic_url` when they are called without options. An application or a library that overrides these two methods is skipped for exactly those calls, while the same helper with any option still goes through the override.

```ruby
# Routes STI subclasses like their base class.
def polymorphic_path(record, options = {})
  super(record.becomes(record.class.base_class), options)
end

polymorphic_path(car, action: :edit)        # => "/vehicles/7/edit"
edit_polymorphic_path(car, format: :json)   # => "/vehicles/7/edit.json"
edit_polymorphic_path(car)
# 8.1:  "/vehicles/7/edit"
# main: NoMethodError: undefined method 'edit_car_path'
```

The prefixed helpers are documented as "a shorthand to `action: "..."` in options", so overriding `polymorphic_path` and `polymorphic_url` has been enough to cover them.

Libraries rely on this. Active Admin's `ResourceController::PolymorphicRoutes` overrides both methods to route records as its named resources, and Inherited Resources (which Active Admin builds on) generates `edit_resource_path` / `new_resource_url` and friends for a polymorphic `belongs_to` by calling the prefixed helpers with an array and an empty options hash. I confirmed both by reading their sources (activeadmin 3.5.2, inherited_resources 2.1.0); I did not run Active Admin against main.

### Detail

This Pull Request changes the prefixed helpers to go through `polymorphic_path` and `polymorphic_url` in every case, as they did until 5bcc222d2b (#59471), which is not in a release. The other allocation savings of #59471 (for arrays) are untouched.

### Additional information

The cost is three objects per call of a prefixed helper without options, measured with `GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)` for a `resources :posts` route:

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `edit_post_path(post)` | 11 | 11 |
| `edit_polymorphic_path(post)` | 11 | 14 |
| `edit_polymorphic_url(post)` | 13 | 16 |
| `polymorphic_path(post, action: :edit)` | 18 | 18 |

The added test overrides `polymorphic_path` and `polymorphic_url` and checks that the four prefixed helpers reach them; it fails on main.

Tests run: `actionview`: `bin/test test/activerecord/polymorphic_routes_test.rb test/template/url_helper_test.rb test/template/form_helper_test.rb test/template/form_helper/form_with_test.rb test/template/navigation_helper_test.rb test/template/record_identifier_test.rb test/activerecord/form_helper_activerecord_test.rb` (846 runs, 0 failures). `actionpack`: `bin/test test/dispatch/routing_test.rb test/controller/url_for_test.rb test/controller/redirect_test.rb test/dispatch/routing/custom_url_helpers_test.rb test/controller/resources_test.rb` (592 runs, 0 failures).

title: Fix #59879: validates_presence_of with allow_nil for belongs_to pointing at a missing record
body:
Fixes #59879.

`validates_presence_of :post, allow_nil: true` on a `belongs_to` association accepted a foreign key pointing at a record that does not exist:

```ruby
Comment.validates_presence_of(:post, allow_nil: true)
Comment.create!(post_id: 98) # no Post with id 98
# => saved, then raised SQLite3::ConstraintException (FOREIGN KEY constraint failed)
```

The association reader returns `nil` both when the foreign key is `nil` and when it points nowhere, and `EachValidator` skipped the validation whenever the value was `nil` and `allow_nil` was set. `ActiveRecord::Validations::PresenceValidator` now overrides `validate` so that, for `belongs_to` associations, `allow_nil` refers to the foreign key: a missing association with a foreign key set is blank, not nil.

Tests:

* Full `activerecord/test/cases/validations/` suite: 130 runs, 0 failures.

title: Fix #59886: Prevent data-modifying CTEs and multiple statements while preventing writes
body:
Fixes #59886.

`while_preventing_writes` classified a query by its first keyword only, so a query starting with `WITH` or `SELECT` could still write:

```sql
WITH x AS (SELECT 'LIMIT') DELETE FROM users
SELECT 1 LIMIT 1; UPDATE users SET name = 'x'
```

The read-query check (`AbstractAdapter.read_query?`, used by the SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL adapters' `write_query?`) now also rejects:

* multiple statements (`;` followed by another statement), and
* data-modifying statements (`INSERT` / `UPDATE` / `DELETE`) hiding inside a common table expression.

String literals, quoted identifiers and comments are stripped before scanning, so keywords and semicolons inside them are not mistaken for SQL — e.g. `SELECT * FROM t WHERE nick = 'a;b'` and `-- DELETE ...\nSELECT ...` still pass.

Tests:

* `activerecord/test/cases/adapter_prevent_writes_test.rb`: 20 runs, 30 assertions, 0 failures (6 new tests).
* `railties/test/commands/query_test.rb`: 33 runs, 81 assertions, 0 failures (2 new tests).
* RuboCop: no offenses on the changed files.

Note: this does not cover `SELECT ... INTO`, which can also write while starting with `SELECT`. Happy to follow up on that separately if wanted.

title: Raise MissingAttributeError when validating a column that was not selected
body:
### Motivation / Background

#56130 changed `ActiveModel::Validations#read_attribute_for_validation` to return `nil` when the record doesn't respond to the attribute, so that errors can be added to attributes that can't be read. But Active Record's `respond_to?` returns `false` for a column that wasn't selected, so validators now read such a column as `nil`.

With `validates :name, presence: true` and `validates :email, format: /@/`:

```ruby
User.select(:id, :confirmed).find_each { |u| u.update(confirmed: true) }
```

|                    | 8.1.4                                          | main                                                      |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `update`           | `MissingAttributeError: missing attribute 'name'` | `false`, nothing is saved                              |
| `update!`          | `MissingAttributeError`                        | `RecordInvalid: Name can't be blank, Email is invalid`    |

So a loop like the one above, which used to fail loudly, now finishes and changes nothing.

### Detail

Active Record now reads columns directly in `read_attribute_for_validation`, so a column that wasn't selected raises `ActiveModel::MissingAttributeError` again. Attributes that are not columns still go through the `nil` fallback from #56130, so `errors.add(:foo_bar, :invalid)` keeps working (there is a test for that on an Active Record model too).

No CHANGELOG entry, because #56130 isn't released yet.

title: `rails query --sql` executes data-modifying CTEs and multiple statements
body:
### Steps to reproduce

`bin/rails query` says it "prevents database writes", and `--sql` "restricts execution to SQL only". When no `reading` role is configured, the only guard is `while_preventing_writes`. That guard classifies a query by its first keyword, so a query that starts with `WITH` or `SELECT` and still writes is executed.

In an app on `main` with the default SQLite database:

```
$ bin/rails runner 'p User.count'
2
$ bin/rails query --sql "UPDATE users SET name = 'x'"
{"error":"Write query attempted while in readonly mode: UPDATE users SET name = 'x' LIMIT 101", ...}
$ bin/rails query --sql "WITH x AS (SELECT 'LIMIT') DELETE FROM users"
{"columns":[],"rows":[],"meta":{"row_count":0, ...}}
$ bin/rails runner 'p User.count'
0
```

On PostgreSQL, the same guard lets these through (checked with `while_preventing_writes { connection.select_all(sql) }`, which is what `--sql` runs):

```sql
WITH d AS (DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM d  -- row is deleted
SELECT 1 LIMIT 1; UPDATE users SET name = 'x'                          -- all rows are updated
```

A plain `UPDATE` raises `ActiveRecord::ReadOnlyError`, as expected.

### Expected behavior

`--sql` cannot change data, as the USAGE says.

### Actual behavior

Data-modifying CTEs (SQLite, PostgreSQL) and multiple statements (PostgreSQL) are executed.

### Notes

The docs of `while_preventing_writes` already say that it "does not provide the same protection as a readonly user". The command is made for LLM agents, and #57420 came from an agent that sent a delete to production through it. So I think the read-only part should be enforced by the database for the duration of the query, for example:

- PostgreSQL / MySQL: run the query in a transaction that starts with `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`.
- SQLite: `PRAGMA query_only = ON`, restored afterwards.

On PostgreSQL, a query with several statements can also end the read-only transaction (`...; COMMIT; DELETE ...`), so it may also need to reject multiple statements (for example, by running the query through the extended protocol).

If that is out of scope, maybe the USAGE could say that writes are only blocked best-effort unless a `reading` role with a read-only user is configured.

cc @lewispb

### System configuration

**Rails version**: main (df8c05111e)

**Ruby version**: 4.0.4

title: Continue flushing idle connections after a disconnect fails
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because `ConnectionPool#flush` stops at the first connection whose `disconnect!` raises. It has already removed every selected idle connection from the pool, so the remaining ones stay open with nothing left to close them.

When the flush runs on the pool reaper, the error also ends the reaper thread. That thread is shared by every pool in the process, so after it dies no pool is reaped, flushed, kept alive or prepopulated until another pool is created.

The built-in adapters guard their own `disconnect!`, so this needs an adapter or driver whose `disconnect!` raises. `ConnectionPool#disconnect` (a8af925c65) and the failed-reset path of `ConnectionPool#reap` (#59843) already handle that case: they report the error and move on to the next connection. `flush` is the remaining place that removes connections from the pool and then disconnects them without doing the same.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (fails on main, passes on this branch)</summary>

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "tmpdir"

database = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, "flush_example.sqlite3")
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(
  adapter: "sqlite3", database: database,
  pool: 2, reaping_frequency: 0.1, idle_timeout: 0.2
)
pool = ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool

# Two connections go idle; the first one has been idle longest.
first = pool.checkout
second = pool.checkout
[first, second].each do |connection|
  connection.select_value("SELECT 1")
  pool.checkin(connection)
end

# None of the built-in adapters raise here; this stands in for an adapter
# or driver whose disconnect! does.
first.define_singleton_method(:disconnect!) { raise ActiveRecord::ConnectionFailed, "disconnect failed" }

reaper = Thread.list.find { |thread| thread.name == "AR Pool Reaper" }
sleep 1

puts "reaper thread alive:          #{reaper.alive?}"
puts "second connection connected:  #{second.connected?}"
puts "connections left in the pool: #{pool.connections.size}"
```

On main, the reaper thread reports `disconnect failed (ActiveRecord::ConnectionFailed)` from `ConnectionPool#flush`, then:

```
reaper thread alive:          false
second connection connected:  true
connections left in the pool: 0
```

On this branch:

```
reaper thread alive:          true
second connection connected:  false
connections left in the pool: 0
```

</details>

### Detail

This Pull Request changes `ConnectionPool#flush` to disconnect each removed connection inside `ActiveSupport.error_reporter.handle(source: "active_record.connection_pool")`, the same call `ConnectionPool#disconnect` uses. A failing `disconnect!` is reported to `Rails.error` and the flush carries on with the next connection.

The new test in `connection_pool_test.rb` runs for both the thread and fiber pool test classes. It makes the longest-idle connection fail to disconnect, then checks that the error is reported and the other connection is still disconnected.

### Additional information

`flush` no longer raises when a connection fails to disconnect, which matches `ConnectionPool#disconnect`. The reaper itself is unchanged; it still stops on errors raised elsewhere in its loop.

body:
### Steps to reproduce

```ruby
Gem.paths = ENV.merge!({ "GEM_HOME" => Gem.user_dir })
require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:

end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"

  config.active_record.encryption.deterministic_key = "deterministic_key"
  config.active_record.encryption.key_derivation_salt = "key_derivation_salt"
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end

  create_table :comments, force: true do |t|
    t.references :post, foreign_key: true
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :comments
end

class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post, optional: true
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  def test_validates_presence
    post = Post.create!(id: 1)

    # We're testing different validator configurations while providing 3
    # different associated ID values:
    # 1. nil
    # 2. blank (non-existent, non-nil ID)
    # 3. existing ID

    # validates :post, presence: true
    Comment.validates_presence_of(:post)
    assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid do
      Comment.create!(post_id: nil)
    end
    assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid do
      Comment.create!(post_id: 98)
    end
    Comment.create!(post_id: post.id)
    Comment.clear_validators!

    # validates :post, presence: {allow_nil: true}
    # BUG when validating blank
    Comment.validates_presence_of(:post, allow_nil: true)
    Comment.create!(post_id: nil)
    assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid do
      # BUG: Blanks are disallowed. This should raise validation exception, but
      # instead causes:
      #   SQLite3::ConstraintException: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
      Comment.create!(post_id: 98)
    end
    Comment.create!(post_id: post.id)
    Comment.clear_validators!

    # validates :post, presence: {allow_blank: true}
    Comment.validates_presence_of(:post, allow_blank: true)
    Comment.create!(post_id: nil)
    assert_raises ActiveRecord::InvalidForeignKey do
      Comment.create!(post_id: 98)
    end
    Comment.create!(post_id: post.id)
    Comment.clear_validators!
  end
end
```

### Expected behavior

With `allow_nil: true` option and default `allow_blank: false` non-nil, non-existent ID should result in validation error.

### Actual behavior

Blank record is accepted and record reported as valid.

It seems like validator does not properly differentiate between _nil_ and _non-nil but blank_ associations.

title: Upload attachments of a record saved again by another instance in the same transaction
body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59877

When several instances of the same record are saved in a transaction, the after-commit callbacks run on only one of them, by default the last one saved (#45280, `run_commit_callbacks_on_first_saved_instances_in_transaction = false` since 7.1). Active Storage uploads new attachments in an after-commit callback of the instance they were attached to, so if another instance of the record is saved later in the same transaction, the attachment and blob rows are committed but the file is never uploaded:

```ruby
User.transaction do
  user = User.create!(avatar: file)
  User.find(user.id).update!(name: "...")
end

user.avatar.download # => ActiveStorage::FileNotFoundError
```

This happens, for example, when a job running inline loads and saves the record inside the transaction that created it.

### Detail

An instance that doesn't run its after-commit callbacks is still sent `committed!(should_run_callbacks: false)`, so `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` now uploads its pending attachment changes there, next to its existing `reload`/`becomes` overrides. Records are committed in the order they were saved, so the earlier instance uploads before the later one runs its after-commit callbacks, and an `after_commit` callback that processes the attachment still finds the file.

I considered uploading through a transaction-level `after_commit` instead, but those run after the records' own after-commit callbacks, so user callbacks that read the attachment would run before the upload.

### Additional information

With `run_commit_callbacks_on_first_saved_instances_in_transaction = true` the reproduction already passes, and it still does with this change. The Active Storage suite passes apart from the existing failures that need ffmpeg and yarn locally, which fail the same way on `main`.

title: Don't mark a serialized attribute changed when it was only encoded differently
body:
### Motivation / Background

`Type::Serialized#changed_in_place?` compares the stored bytes with a fresh encoding of the value. A row whose bytes the coder wouldn't produce today is therefore reported as changed as soon as the attribute is read, even though nothing was modified.

Since #58612 (99a9ba3fe5), that includes every `store` or `serialize coder: ActiveRecord::Coders::JSON` row containing `<`, `>` or `&` that was written before 8.1.4. Earlier versions wrote those characters HTML-escaped. Reproduced with the released gems on PostgreSQL:

```ruby
class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  store :settings, accessors: [:title], coder: ActiveRecord::Coders::JSON
end

# written by activerecord 8.1.3:   {"title":"Tom & Jerry <3"}
post = Post.first   # read by activerecord 8.1.4
post.title
post.changed?        # => true  (false on 8.1.3)
post.changed         # => ["settings"]
```

The same happens to JSON a database writes itself; `jsonb::text` yields `{"identified": true}`. It costs more than an extra write. Saving issues an UPDATE that touches `updated_at` and runs update callbacks. And `Attached::One#attach` defers saving a record that already has changes, so for an Active Storage blob whose metadata reads as changed, `blob.preview_image.attach(...)` never saves.

### Detail

When the stored and new bytes differ, `changed_in_place?` now re-encodes the stored value with the current coder before concluding it changed. A record counts as changed only if the bytes the coder would write now differ from what it would write for the stored value.

- Nothing changes when the bytes already match, so the common path does the same work as before.
- Differences the coder itself would write still count as changes. Hash key order still counts, so `test_changed_in_place_compare_serialized_representation` still passes, and so do `1` vs `1.0` and real mutations. The new tests pin both.
- No equality method on the deserialized object is involved, unlike the opt-in `comparable:` from 6a71a2ffea, so this is safe for any coder.

### Additional information

The new tests in `serialized_attribute_test.rb` and `blob_test.rb` fail without the change. Run locally:

- **SQLite:** `serialized_attribute_test`, `store_test`, `dirty_test`, `attribute_methods_test`, the coder, JSON and encryption tests. 660 runs, 0 failures.
- **PostgreSQL:** `serialized_attribute_test`, `dirty_test`, the JSON, hstore and encryption tests. 505 runs, 0 failures.
- **Active Storage:** `test/models`. 193 runs, 0 failures.

title: Add `config.action_cable.allow_missing_origin`
body:
### Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because Action Cable rejects every WebSocket handshake that has no `Origin` header. Browsers always send one, but clients that aren't browsers (mobile apps, devices, other servers, Postman) often don't. The advice they usually get, including in #31524, is to set `config.action_cable.disable_request_forgery_protection = true`, which turns the origin check off for browsers too.

Proposed in https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/91694.

### Detail

This Pull Request adds `config.action_cable.allow_missing_origin`, off by default.

When it's on, a handshake with no `Origin` header is accepted. A handshake that has the header goes through `allow_same_origin_as_host` and `allowed_request_origins` exactly as before, so `Origin: null`, an empty `Origin` and origins that aren't allowed are still rejected.

It also changes what's logged when a handshake is rejected for having no `Origin` header. Today the line ends in a blank (`Request origin not allowed: `). Now it says the header is missing and names the option.

The option is documented in the Action Cable Overview and Configuring guides.

### Additional information

**Why off by default.** The origin check stops cross-site WebSocket hijacking, which needs a browser, and browsers always send `Origin` on a WebSocket handshake (RFC 6455 [§4.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1), [§10.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-10.2)). The one case where accepting a missing `Origin` lets that attack through is a browser whose header was stripped on the way. That is the reasoning behind the `:header_only` default for new 8.2 apps in Action Controller (#56350), which rejects a non-GET request over HTTPS that has no `Sec-Fetch-Site`. So this is opt-in rather than a new default. Turning it on through `load_defaults` would be a small follow-up if that's ever wanted.

**Why not only document `allowed_request_origins = [nil, ...]`**, which works today. Few people find it (in #31524 users found it by trial and error), and setting `allowed_request_origins` in `config/application.rb` drops the development default of `/https?:\/\/localhost:\d+/`, because the engine applies that default with `||=`. The new option leaves `allowed_request_origins` alone. A test now covers the `nil` workaround, so it keeps working.

title: Allow ActionController::Live to stop copying thread locals
body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59733.

`ActionController::Live#process` copies every `Thread.current[]` entry of the request thread to the thread running the action. Only references are copied, so any mutable object stored in a thread local becomes shared between two threads that run concurrently. This breaks code that uses thread locals precisely to avoid sharing state, and it's hard to diagnose because it only happens in controllers that include `Live`.

Related reports over the years (#13547, #17428, #21209, #52906, #58870) all come from this behavior. #52906 and #58870 were addressed by excluding or protecting specific keys (`live_streaming_excluded_keys`, #58881), but the blanket copy of `Thread.current` is still there.

### Detail

This Pull Request adds `config.action_controller.live_streaming_copy_thread_locals`:

- `true` (current behavior): thread locals are copied to the streaming thread.
- `false`: the streaming thread starts with its own thread locals and only inherits `ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState` (which backs `ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes`), still honoring `live_streaming_excluded_keys`.

Like `live_streaming_excluded_keys`, it can also be set per controller (`self.live_streaming_copy_thread_locals = false`).

The default stays `true` for existing applications and becomes `false` with `load_defaults "8.2"`. The option is documented in the `ActionController::Live` API docs, the configuring guide, and `new_framework_defaults_8_2.rb`.

### Additional information

**Upgrade impact:** apps that set a thread local *before* the controller runs (e.g. in a middleware, or via gems such as `request_store`) and read it during a streamed action won't see it with the new default. They can keep the old behavior by setting the option to `true`, or move that state to `ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes` / `ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState`, which are still propagated. State set inside the action itself (including `before_action` / `around_action` callbacks) isn't affected, since callbacks already run in the streaming thread.

**Alternatives considered:**

- *Removing the copy outright*: simplest, but it breaks the existing behavior without an opt-out.
- *An allowlist of keys to copy*: closer to the "owner-controlled propagation" suggested in the issue, but it adds more API surface, and `IsolatedExecutionState` / `CurrentAttributes` already provide an explicit way to propagate context.
- *`dup`/`deep_dup` of the values*: as noted in the issue, Rails can't infer the copy semantics of arbitrary objects.

In #52906 it was mentioned that changing these defaults should happen in a future version, possibly with a deprecation. I went with a new framework default; I'm happy to add a deprecation path instead if that's preferred.

title: Disconnect when a thread is killed during configure_connection
body:
### Motivation / Background

When a thread is killed with `Thread#kill` while Active Record sets up a new connection's session (`configure_connection`), and the thread returns the connection to the pool on its way out, the next thread that checks the connection out runs on a session that was never fully set up. On PostgreSQL every query on that connection then raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'key?' for nil` (the result type map was never loaded). On SQLite the pragmas are SQLite's defaults, so foreign keys are not enforced and the journal is not WAL. Nothing raises on SQLite. It lasts until the connection is reconnected.

#54711 made `attempt_configure_connection` disconnect the adapter when setup fails, and #54738 widened its `rescue` to `Exception` so `Timeout.timeout` is covered too. A killed thread skips `rescue` and runs only `ensure` blocks, so the adapter keeps its raw connection and stays marked as verified. Returning the connection is ordinary: `with_connection` does it in an `ensure`, and so does the executor at the end of a request or job.

Threads get killed while the process goes on using the pool, for example:

- the parallel gem's `in_threads` kills its worker threads when its caller is interrupted, e.g. by a request timeout,
- job workers built on `Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor` kill threads still running after their shutdown timeout, and Puma kills them after `force_shutdown_after`. Here the pool is only used again if the process keeps running.

What keeps a thread in session setup is a database that is slow to answer at that moment.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (fails on main, passes on this branch)</summary>

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "tmpdir"

database = File.join(Dir.mktmpdir, "development.sqlite3")
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: database, pool: 1, timeout: 5000)
pool = ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool

# Another process holds the write lock (a migration, a backup), so session
# setup waits in `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`.
blocker = SQLite3::Database.new(database)
blocker.execute("BEGIN EXCLUSIVE")

request = Thread.new do
  pool.with_connection { |connection| connection.select_value("SELECT 1") }
end
sleep 0.01 until request.backtrace&.any? { |line| line.match?(/[#`]configure_connection'/) }
request.kill.join # an app server or job worker stopping after its shutdown timeout
blocker.execute("ROLLBACK")

pool.with_connection do |connection|
  puts "journal_mode=#{connection.select_value("PRAGMA journal_mode")} " \
    "foreign_keys=#{connection.select_value("PRAGMA foreign_keys")}"
end
```

On main:

```
journal_mode=delete foreign_keys=0
```

On this branch:

```
journal_mode=wal foreign_keys=1
```

</details>

### Detail

This Pull Request moves the cleanup in `attempt_configure_connection` from a `rescue Exception` to an `ensure`, which disconnects unless the block completed. It still returns the block's value. It also disconnects when the block is left by `throw` or a non-local `return`, which nothing in Rails does today.

### Additional information

The test kills a thread inside `configure_connection` and checks that the next query on the connection sets the session up again. It fails without the change on SQLite and PostgreSQL. The Active Record suite passes on SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL was not run, but the change is in `AbstractAdapter`, which the MySQL adapters share.

I also reproduced this with a real PostgreSQL server made slow by a proxy, with `with_connection` on main, 8.1.4.1, 8.0.5.2, 7.2.4 and 7.1.6, and with a release in an `ensure` on main and 8.1.4.1. On main I also tried a `Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor` job worker that is shut down and then killed, and the parallel gem under `Timeout.timeout`; both fail the same way. Puma's forced shutdown was only tried with a second server in the same process, which isn't how Puma restarts. A thread that leases a connection and never returns it is not affected: the reaper resets it.

#59567 also changes `attempt_configure_connection`. The two changes don't overlap in behaviour, but whichever lands second needs a small rebase.

title: `rails new` raises `Unrecognized command "solid_cache:install"` when a template removes `solid_cache` from the Gemfile
body:
### Steps to reproduce

`run_solid` in `railties/lib/rails/generators/app_base.rb` runs every Solid installer in one command, whether or not the gem is in the generated `Gemfile`:

```ruby
commands = "solid_cache:install solid_queue:install"
commands += " solid_cable:install" unless skip_action_cable?

rails_command commands
```

An application template runs before `run_solid`, so it can remove a Solid gem from the `Gemfile`. Save this as `remove_solid_cache.rb`:

```ruby
gsub_file "Gemfile", /^gem "solid_cache"\n/, ""
```

Then generate an application with it:

```bash
rails new myapp --main -m remove_solid_cache.rb
```

### Expected behavior

The generator runs `solid_queue:install` and `solid_cable:install` for the gems that are still in the `Gemfile`, and skips `solid_cache:install`.

### Actual behavior

`bin/rails solid_cache:install solid_queue:install solid_cable:install` aborts on the first command, because the application does not load `solid_cache`, and generation stops:

```text
Unrecognized command "solid_cache:install" (Rails::Command::UnrecognizedCommandError)
Did you mean?  solid_queue:install
               solid_cable:install
```

The same happens for any partial Solid setup, such as a template that keeps only one of the three gems.

### System configuration

**Rails version**: `main` at 78f4f0df59866e8951646183c1f275e186916ba7

**Ruby version**: 3.4.8

A fix is proposed in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/57037.

title: Quote `Rational` values as floats
body:
### Motivation / Background

`Rational#to_s` returns a fraction, so `quote(Rational(1, 2))` produces `1/2`. PostgreSQL and SQLite evaluate that with integer division, so the value silently becomes `0`:

```ruby
# SQLite, prepared_statements: false
Item.create!(price: 0.25)
Item.where("price < ?", Rational(1, 2)).count # => 0, expected 1
Item.sanitize_sql_array(["price < ?", Rational(1, 2)]) # => "price < 1/2"
```

This affects every path that quotes values into the SQL rather than binding them: unprepared statements, `sanitize_sql_array`, and `connection.quote`.

### Detail

#44404 fixed this for MySQL by casting bound Rationals with `to_f`. The PostgreSQL and SQLite adapters' `type_cast` methods already use `to_f` for bind parameters. This applies the same conversion in the abstract `quote`, so quoted and bound Rationals agree on every adapter.

The existing PostgreSQL and SQLite tests asserting `"3/4"` and `"0/1"` were updated. They were brought over from the MySQL tests and recorded the previous output rather than an intended behavior.

### Additional information

`to_f` can lose precision for some Rationals. This matches the existing MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite bind behavior, and is closer to the intended value than integer division.

title: Read by name for attributes whose slot moved after reset_column_information
body:
### Motivation / Background

Fixes #59831

Since #59141 the generated readers read by slot, and the slot is fixed when the reader is defined. A record loaded before `reset_column_information` keeps its old layout, so once the readers are defined again, a reader whose attribute moved to another slot reads the wrong value. In the issue, `user.name` returns the removed `legacy` column, and keeps returning it after `user.name = "changed"`, so a data migration could save the wrong value without an error.

### Detail

This follows the approach @seyhunak suggested in the issue, which keeps the read path unchanged. The model remembers the slot each attribute's reader was first defined with. When the readers are defined again, an attribute whose slot changed gets a reader that reads by name (the reader from before #59141), and every other attribute keeps reading by slot. Every record defines the attribute methods when it's initialized, so any layout a loaded record has is one the readers were defined with.

Slots move when a column is removed, and also when a column is added, since columns come before the attributes declared with `attribute` in the layout. Once an attribute has moved it keeps the by-name reader, even if it moves back to its first slot (a declared attribute after a column is added and then removed), because records from the layout in between may still be around.

Models whose schema isn't changed at runtime never get a by-name reader, and the slot reader is unchanged.

The regression tests in `hot_compatibility_test.rb` cover records loaded before a column is removed (read and write), before a column is added, with extra select columns, and declared attributes that move and move back. The teardown now also clears the model's cached columns, since a test that calls `reset_column_information` after removing a column would otherwise leave them stale for the next test.

### Additional information

Reads cost the same for models whose attributes don't move, since their generated reader is unchanged. On my machine with YJIT (5M reads, two runs each, the differences are noise):

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `record.name` | 65.2 to 69.9 ns | 64.2 to 64.8 ns |
| record loaded with `select("users.*, 1 AS one")` | 65.1 to 65.2 ns | 64.1 to 64.4 ns |

The full Active Record suite passes on SQLite. I couldn't run the Ractor suite locally: it fails to boot on `main` with Ruby 3.4 (`main_connection_handler` NameError in `RactorConnectionHandler`). The new state is only read and written while the attribute methods are being defined, like `@attribute_methods_generated`.
